Three ways to get a more precise treatment effect out of a sample you cannot
grow. All of them work by choosing *which* random split you end up with,
rather than by collecting more units.

<!-- Both claims below are computed in the articles. If the datasets or seeds
     change, re-check them:
       400 -> 1,200  -> posts/pairwise-matching, "What it is worth on two real
                        datasets" (the Project STAR sample)
       worse off     -> posts/pairwise-matching, "Analysing a matched
                        experiment" and "A conservative interval is not always
                        a safe one" -->

::: {.keybox}
**Pair 400 pupils on last year's test scores, then flip the coin inside each
pair: as precise as 1,200 pupils.**
:::

::: {.keybox}
**Match your sample, then analyse it the standard way, and you can end up
worse off than not matching.**
:::

Pairwise matching and rerandomization are the two methods. The Mahalanobis
distance is the measure of "alike" that both are built on, and is worth
reading when you want to know why correlated covariates are counted once, or
what makes the distance fail quietly.

All the code is Python, every figure is reproducible from the source, and the
whole thing lives in
[the repository](https://github.com/AlexanderDBolton/BoostSampleSize).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Series status

*Pairwise matching*, *Rerandomization* and *The Mahalanobis distance* are
written. *Stratification* exists as an outline and is not yet published.
:::
